newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada hopes for Zaire decision "in day or so".
newsitem.headline: Canada hopes for Zaire decision "in day or so".

text.p: Canada hopes to reach international consensus in the next day or so on moving ahead with the long-awaited humanitarian mission for central Africa, Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Monday.

"The hope is that we can arrive at an agreement amongst the various coalition partners within a matter of a day or so," Axworthy told Parliament when asked how many more meetings would be needed before refugees would be helped.
"The meetings that were held last week were very important in terms of determining what the needs were," Axworthy said.
His spokeswoman, Catherine Lappe, told reporters later they should emphasise the "or so" -- meaning it might take more than 24 hours.

"We are ... presently talking to a number of the coalition partners to determine exactly what the most appropriate response would be based upon the information that was arrived at this weekend," Axworthy said.

He has called about a dozen foreign ministers from Africa and Europe, including those of France, Britain, Spain, the Netherlands, South Africa, Cameroon, Ireland and the Organisation of African Unity, Lappe said.

The U.N. Security Council authorised a mission to eastern Zaire on Nov. 15 to assist refugees and displaced Zaireans, but the subsequent return of half a million to Rwanda has caused a lengthy reassessment.

Axworthy told Parliament he shared the frustration of many with the time it was taking to launch the mission, but added: "We can't move by ourselves. We must move in partnership with the other members of the coalition."
The Canadian government appeared to be leaning toward mounting some sort of military force, heavily scaled back, to help the refugees and displaced people still left in Zaire.

"My view is we have to be ready for a military intervention," Prime Minister Jean Chretien, who assembled much of the international support for the mission in the first place, told a news conference in the Philippines.
Chretien, who also spoke about the issue with President Bill Clinton while in Manila, said a force in the range of 1,000 to 1,500 troops might be enough, rather than the originally planned 10,000.
Besides the Nov. 15 Security Council meeting, diplomats met in New York on Wednesday, military planners met on Friday through Sunday in Stuttgart, and aid officials met in Geneva on Saturday.

The meeting in Stuttgart set out various scenarios but did not settle on any or where the mission would be based. Rwanda says a military force would be unwelcome, leading to speculation Uganda might be chosen as a base.
In Washington, meanwhile, Canadian Defence Minister Doug Young was discussing Zaire with his U.S. counterpart, William Perry.

Lappe said that if a military force were settled on, officials from the participating nations would probably have to meet as a steering board or contact group, but she said this could be done quickly in New York.
International Cooperation Minister Don Boudria, just back from the Geneva aid meeting, told Parliament another such meeting would be held in a few days, hopefully in the Rwandan capital Kigali.
The delays prompted an outburst in Brussels from French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who asserted the world was dragging its feet because it did not care about Africa.
"I am frankly shocked when I see that kind of apathy hiding behind endless discussions," he told reporters.
